Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette:
At seventy-eight, George had lived alone since his divorce twenty years ago, managing his health and his part-time database consulting work from the quiet suburban house he’d bought in the nineties. Two years ago, a crushing sensation in his chest during a late-night data migration session sent him to the emergency room, where he was diagnosed with a massive myocardial infarction. The stent insertion was successful, but the experience—the sudden pain, the frantic ambulance ride, the antiseptic-and-metal smell of the cath lab—left something behind that no medication could touch. Even now, months later, that odor can ambush him without warning: the sharp, clean scent of isopropyl alcohol from a hand sanitizer, or the metallic tang of a blood pressure cuff, and suddenly he is back on the gurney, the lights blurring overhead, his heart slamming against his ribs as if it were happening right now. These memories are not like ordinary recollections; they are more real and vivid than the chair he is sitting in, flooding him with the same terror he felt when the doctor said the words “blockage” and “emergency bypass” and he was certain he would never leave the hospital alive.

In the months following his discharge, George noticed a change in how he experienced his own home. The house he had always considered a sanctuary now felt like a stage where a second attack could occur. He became hypervigilant, checking his pulse on the side of his neck at every faint twinge, listening to his own breathing at night. Even when he knew he was medically stable—his cardiologist had assured him—his body kept reacting as if the danger were still immediate, a trembling readiness that he could not will away. He began to feel a deep, corrosive shame: he was supposed to have taken better care of himself, to have noticed the warning signs earlier. The guilt mixed with a raw fear that anything—a sudden sound, a change in temperature, a strong smell—could signal the beginning of another event.

The constant state of alertness gradually reshaped how George saw the world. When he found himself scanning his living room for potential hazards—a misplaced rug he might trip on, a room that seemed too warm—he could not escape the conclusion that the world was fundamentally dangerous, a place where safety was an illusion. Each intrusive memory, especially the olfactory flashbacks, reinforced that belief. The metallic scent that seized him in the supermarket aisle or the antiseptic smell that hit him in his own bathroom would bring the reliving to life, and afterward he would find himself thinking that his body was a traitor, that life itself could never be trusted again. He lost his faith in the idea that people or institutions could protect him; the doctors had saved him, but they could not guarantee tomorrow. The church he had attended occasionally now felt hollow, and he stopped returning the calls of his old friends because they did not understand that the world had changed—that he lived in a constant state of threat, and that his memories had become more real than the present.

The consequences accumulated. George stopped accepting new database projects from his former employer because the concentration he needed for writing queries was shattered by sudden flashbacks. He became wary of leaving his home office, spending most of his time in a single chair near the window where he could see the driveway. His daughter, who visited every Sunday, began to notice that he would not let her cook in the kitchen because the smell of searing meat reminded him of something he could not name. He knew he was isolating himself, but the only safe path seemed to be minimizing exposure to any sensation that could trigger the reliving—and that meant staying still, staying quiet, staying hypervigilant.

What finally brought George to therapy was a panic attack in the produce aisle of his local grocery store. The scent of green peppers—why green peppers?—had hit him with such force that he felt his heart rate spike, his vision tunnel, and he was certain he was dying again. His daughter found him sitting on a crate near the checkout, trembling, and she insisted he talk to someone. George came to the first session with a single question: “How do I stop being afraid of my own body?” He was afraid that his hypervigilance would never end, that the flashbacks would keep pulling him backward, and that he had already lost too much years he could have spent feeling safe. But beneath that fear was a small hope: that a therapist might show him a world that was not as dangerous as his memories and his body insisted it was.
